paper_title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Robot leading is an active humanrobot navigation task in which robot guides designated follower along an intended route to target destination, with applications in airports, retail spaces, campuses, and other public environments. During leading, the follower may slow down, stop, fall behind, become temporarily unobservable, or briefly disengage, requiring the robot to adapt without losing the intended route. The task therefore requires both reliable route execution and responsive humanrobot interaction. Existing robot-leading systems have made substantial progress on both aspects. Classical methods typically rely on explicit geometric representations, interaction rules, and planning logic [13], while learning-based approaches increasingly learn follower dynamics or guiding behavior from data [4, 5]. More recently, foundation models have introduced richer language grounding and semantic understanding [68], yet follower understanding and physical route execution are still often connected through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces [9]. In contrast, people naturally adjust their pace and local motion to follower while preserving the intended route. This motivates direct embodied learning question: can robot learn unified policy that executes given route while adapting its actions to designated follower? natural intuition is to predict the complete leading trajectory end-to-end from route, visual, and language inputs. However, we observe that this direct formulation can entangle route execution with follower response: changes in follower behavior that should mainly affect execution may also distort the underlying route geometry. This motivates simple structured formulation: preserve the route as stable execution reference while learning how to adapt its execution to the follower and local scene. Based on this idea, we introduce LeadVLA, which uses the given route as an explicit Path reference, learned Pace to regulate progress along it, and Residual for local followerand scene-conditioned adaptation. Learning follower-aware route execution at scale also requires suitable training supervision and closed-loop Figure 1 Keep the route, adapt the execution. robot leads language-designated tourist to the departure terminal along planned route. The sequence shows (1) normal leading, (2) slowing down as the follower pauses for phone call, (3) waiting while the follower briefly disengages to interact with another pedestrian, and (4) resuming afterward. The nominal route remains unchanged, while the robot adapts how it executes the route to the followers evolving behavior. evaluation. Existing public resources do not yet jointly provide scalable action-level supervision and standardized evaluation tailored to this setting [7, 10, 11]. We therefore develop LeadInfra, configurable Unreal Engine-based infrastructure that composes diverse routes, scenes, follower behaviors, and singleor multi-person configurations into closed-loop robot-leading episodes, together with LeadBench, standardized closed-loop benchmark. For this work, we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus with LeadInfra and evaluate on 108 fully held-out LeadBench episodes from disjoint environments, routes, actors, and scene instantiations under the same task definition and interaction contract. On LeadBench, LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness. Real-world closed-loop experiments further show transfer to unseen environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Our main contributions are: (1) We formulate robot leading as follower-aware route-execution problem and introduce LeadVLA, which preserves the route as stable execution reference while learning follower-aware adaptation. (2) We develop LeadInfra and LeadBench, providing scalable closed-loop interaction supervision and standardized evaluation for follower-aware robot leading. (3) We validate the formulation through controlled closed-loop experiments and real-robot deployment, and will release LeadVLA checkpoints, LeadInfra, and LeadBench to support continued research.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Robot Leading Methods. Robot leading has progressed from explicitly designed human-aware navigation toward increasingly learned and foundation-model-based systems. Early methods coupled route execution with follower state through geometric planners, interaction rules, or probabilistic models [13]. Learningbased methods later learned follower dynamics or guiding policies from data, but typically relied on structured geometric or task representations [4, 5, 12, 13]. More recently, foundation models have introduced richer language grounding, spatial reasoning, and semantic understanding, while continuous physical execution often remains mediated by separate planning or control modules [68, 14]. LeadVLA instead studies how follower understanding and route execution can be coupled within unified multimodal policy while retaining the route as an explicit execution reference. Embodied Navigation. Existing embodied navigation spans goalor instruction-driven navigation, where the robot primarily acts toward specified destination [1517], and person following, where the observed person largely determines robot motion [18, 19]. Recent navigation foundation models further show that multimodal policies can directly predict navigation actions or trajectories from visual and language inputs [20, 21]. Robot leading differs in retaining its own route-level task intent while the designated follower primarily modulates how that route is executed rather than defining the task-level destination or route. Data and Evaluation for Robot Leading. Existing resources cover humanguide interaction, person perception, and spatial or semantic understanding [7, 10, 11, 22, 23], while broader social-navigation simulators provide dynamic human environments and standardized evaluation [24, 25]. Complete guide-robot systems have also been evaluated on route following, obstacle avoidance, and user-centered interaction [35]. However, these resources do not jointly provide scalable action-level supervision and common closed-loop protocol for language-designated follower-aware route execution. LeadInfra and LeadBench target this policy-learning and evaluation layer.

sections.title: 3.3 Follower-Aware Representation and Selective Coupling
sections.content: The structured action space defines how adaptation is expressed; we next supervise what follower information the shared action representation should capture. We use six lightweight auxiliary heads. Target localization supports grounding of the language-designated follower; lateral and distance capture relative geometry; observation and motion capture temporal presence and movement; and formation indicates whether the requested robotfollower relation is being acquired, maintained, or corrected. These objectives supervise the shared representation Qt directly rather than forming an explicit follower-state vector for separate controller. Selective Semantic Coupling. All six objectives shape Qt, but only the predicted lateral and formation distributions are explicitly fused into Residual, as these cues are most directly aligned with local spatial correction. sections.title: 3.4 Referent-Aware Co-training
sections.content: In multi-person scenes, follower-aware control must also determine whose behavior should influence action. Because the follower is specified by language, the policy should respond to the designated person rather than nearby distractors. Counterfactual Referent Pairs. We preserve the route, scene, actors, and behavior while changing only which person is designated by language. The same physical event can therefore require different actions: Figure 5 Progressive LeadBench evaluation. Columns increase route-execution difficulty from clean conditions (Core) to moderate (Easy) and stronger interference (Constrained); rows compare single-person leading with multiperson cases containing distractors. The progression increasingly couples local route recovery with follower-aware control. designated follower stopping should induce slowing or waiting, whereas the same behavior from distractor should not. These matched pairs supervise target-conditioned action attribution. Dynamic Target Reassignment. In selected episodes, the language instruction changes the designated follower while both people remain in the scene. The policy must then update which persons behavior controls subsequent execution rather than remain attached to the previous referent. Together, counterfactual pairs supervise which person should influence action, while reassignment requires this attribution to update online. Joint Training Objective. These interventions modify training supervision without introducing referentspecific loss. LeadVLA uses the same joint objective = Lact + λsemLsem, with λsem = 0.25. The action objective supervises waypoint prediction, Pace, Residual, and regularization, while the semantic objective supervises the six auxiliary heads. Detailed losses and training configuration are provided in Appendix A.4.

sections.title: 3.5 LeadInfra and LeadBench
sections.content: LeadInfra. To provide scalable supervision for follower-aware route execution, we develop LeadInfra, configurable infrastructure for generating closed-loop robot-leading data. As illustrated in Fig. 4, LeadInfra composes route geometry, scene conditions, local interference, follower motion and visibility, requested formation, appearance, and singleor multi-person configurations. Recombining these factors across routes and scenes encourages follower-conditioned execution rather than memorization of fixed trajectory patterns. key design is causal expert supervision from realized interaction evidence. Follower behaviors are scripted, but their hidden labels are never exposed to the robot expert: for example, scripted stop triggers no immediate response, and the expert reacts only after observable consequences such as increasing separation or sustained target loss emerge. Robot actions are therefore supervised from realized interaction rather than hidden future behavior programs. For this work, we instantiate approximately 4M training samples over roughly 1K nominal routes and more than 65K m2 of navigable indoor and outdoor environments. The corpus covers 8 follower-motion programs, 5 presence and reacquisition conditions, 6 language-conditioned formations, and singleand multi-person interactions, yielding 240 nominal motionpresenceformation combinations before additional route, appearance, referent, and scene variation. Further details are provided in Appendix B. LeadBench. To provide standardized evaluation, we develop LeadBench, frozen closed-loop benchmark in which all policies face the same routes, actors, interaction conditions, instructions, and evaluation events under common policy-visible information boundary. Each policy action changes subsequent states and observations; in multi-person cases, matched counterfactual rollouts keep the scene and human behavior fixed while changing only the language-designated follower. LeadBench is disjoint from LeadInfra training in environments, routes, human actors, and scene instantiations while retaining the same task definition and interaction contract. Progressive Evaluation Conditions. LeadBench contains 108 held-out episodes across Core, Easy, and Constrained, which respectively introduce no additional, moderate, and stronger repeated route interference; each includes singleand multi-person settings. Evaluation Metrics. We report Lead Success Rate (LSR) for joint robotfollower completion, Route Fidelity (RF) for route preservation and forward progress, Target Response Score (TRS) for designatedfollower response, and Social Contract Score (SCS) for instructed distance and formation. Detailed definitions, aggregation rules, and termination conditions are provided in Appendix C.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Evaluation protocol. We evaluate all methods in closed loop under the frozen LeadBench protocol. All methods face the same predefined episode conditions, policy-visible information boundary, and common execution environment. We report LSR, RF, TRS, and SCS as defined in Sec. 3.5, with detailed metric definitions, aggregation rules, and termination conditions provided in Appendix C. Baselines. We compare against representative robot-guiding paradigms. Fiore-style controller [1] represents classical modular guiding with explicit follower-state reasoning and geometric route execution. Nanavati et al. [26] and Kästner et al. [13] represent hybrid approaches that combine learned human interaction or navigation with structured route/follower representations. Uni-NaVid-FT [27] represents foundation-modelbased navigation fine-tuned on LeadInfra. We additionally use StarVLA [28] as matched direct-trajectory architectural control: it uses the same Qwen3-VL backbone, temporal observations, route/language inputs, prediction horizon, LeadInfra training data, and optimization budget as LeadVLA, but directly predicts the complete waypoint trajectory without PathPaceResidual composition. We also report Human Expert reference obtained by averaging the results of three human operators evaluated under the same policy-visible observations. All trainable baselines use the same LeadInfra training split when applicable. Implementation details and baseline adaptations are provided in Appendix D.1, and the Human Expert protocol is described in Appendix D.2.

sections.title: 4.2 Overall Performance on LeadBench
sections.content: Table 1 shows that LeadVLA achieves the highest overall task success among the evaluated robot policies while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness. The Fiore-style modular method preserves the nominal route particularly well and performs strongly under clean conditions, but achieves lower TRS and SCS, with task success degrading as route interference increases. In contrast, the matched StarVLA control shows competitive follower responsiveness but degrades more noticeably in route fidelity and task success as execution becomes harder. These trends are consistent with our motivating observation: retaining the route as an explicit execution reference helps preserve route-level task intent, while learned Pace and Residual provide the flexibility needed for followerand scene-conditioned adaptation. The benefit becomes particularly evident in the single-person setting under stronger route interference. LeadVLA maintains an LSR of 0.50 from Easy to Constrained, while Fiore drops from 0.42 to 0.08 and StarVLA from 0.33 to 0.08. At the same time, the task remains far from solved: in the Constrained multi-person setting, LeadVLA reaches only 0.04 LSR compared with 0.75 for the Human Expert, highlighting the remaining difficulty of jointly handling route interference, follower interaction, and referent ambiguity. sections.title: 4.3 Design Analysis and Ablations
sections.content: We evaluate three key design choices of LeadVLA through controlled studies on structured route execution, follower-aware semantic learning and coupling, and referent-aware co-training. All variants share the same Qwen3-VL backbone, LeadInfra training data, optimization budget, and LeadBench protocol. Finergrained difficulty and response-attribution analyses are provided in Appendix D.3, with branch-wise semanticcoupling ablations in Appendix D.4. Does structured route execution matter? We compare direct end-to-end trajectory prediction with Path + Pace and the full Path + Pace + Residual formulation. As shown in Table 2, introducing Path + Pace increases LSR from 0.174 to 0.354 and RF from 0.663 to 0.988, showing the benefit of retaining the route as an explicit execution reference. Adding Residual further improves LSR to 0.396 and SCS to 0.250, while reducing RF as the policy gains flexibility for local deviations. Together, these results support the intended division of roles: Path and Pace stabilize route execution, while Residual provides the local flexibility needed for followerand scene-conditioned adaptation. Core-S 16/20 0.95 0.320 0.210 Core-M 12/20 0.95 0.305 0.195 Easy-S 10/20 0.90 0.285 0.165 Easy-M 4/20 0.80 0.280 0.150 Setting SR RF TRS SCS How should follower semantics influence action? With the structured action formulation fixed, we compare semantic supervision alone, direct fusion of all predicted semantics, and the proposed selective coupling. Table 3 shows that auxiliary supervision improves RF and TRS but does not by itself improve LSR, indicating that semantic supervision alone does not necessarily translate into better task completion. Selective Fusion achieves the highest LSR and SCS among these variants, supporting our design in which semantic objectives broadly shape the shared representation, while direct semantic-to-action coupling is restricted according to the intended control role. Additional difficulty and branch-wise coupling analyses are provided in Appendices D.3 and D.4. Does referent-aware co-training improve control attribution? Table 4 compares training without referent intervention, with either counterfactual pairs or dynamic reassignment alone, and with both together. All variants use matched total training scale, sampling budget, and optimization settings. Either intervention alone yields modest gains in overall task performance, whereas combining both increases LSR from 0.112 to 0.396. The two forms of supervision address complementary aspects of referent-conditioned control: counterfactual pairs teach whose behavior should influence action, while reassignment teaches the policy to update this attribution when the language referent changes. Consistent with this interpretation, the response-attribution analysis in Appendix D.3 shows that target-attributed behavior changes increase from 60.0% without intervention to 86.7% with full co-training. sections.title: 4.4 Sim-to-Real Transfer without Real-World Policy Fine-Tuning
sections.content: We evaluate whether follower-aware route execution learned entirely in simulation transfers to physical deployment. LeadVLA is deployed directly on Unitree G1 humanoid in previously unseen real-world environments, without real-world policy fine-tuning. The real-world settings retain the same core interaction structure as LeadBench, with simplified route-interference and single-/multi-person conditions. We evaluate Core-S, CoreM, Easy-S, and Easy-M with 20 closed-loop trials each, using the same front/rear RGB, language, and route interface as in simulation. At each policy query, LeadVLA predicts 24-step robot-local trajectory that is executed by the robots native trajectory-tracking controller without obstacle replanning or modification of the frozen global route. Inference takes approximately 100200 ms on an NVIDIA GPU server, while SCS is computed offline from RealSense D455 depth. Detailed deployment, route construction, controller interfaces, and real-world metric implementation are provided in Appendix E.1. As shown in Fig. 6 and Table 5, LeadVLA transfers follower-aware route execution across all four realworld settings without real-world policy fine-tuning. Route fidelity remains high across all settings (0.80 0.95 RF), while the policy retains follower-responsive behavior in both singleand multi-person interactions. Performance decreases under stronger route interference, indicating that robust real-world leading remains challenging, but these results demonstrate that the route-execution and follower-response behaviors learned from LeadInfra can transfer to previously unseen physical environments. Additional qualitative analysis and failure cases are provided in Appendix E; more real-world demonstration videos are available on our project page.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.content: We studied robot leading as follower-aware route-execution problem, where robot must preserve routelevel task intent while adapting its execution to designated follower. LeadVLA explores simple structured formulation for this problem: keep the given route as stable Path reference, while learning through Pace and Residual when and how its execution should adapt to the follower and local scene. Together with LeadInfra and LeadBench, we provide unified learning and evaluation framework for studying closed-loop followeraware robot leading. Across controlled experiments, LeadVLA achieves the highest task success among the evaluated robot policies on LeadBench and transfers to previously unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Robot leading nevertheless remains far from solved. Performance degrades when strong route interference, multi-person interaction, and referent ambiguity must be handled simultaneously, leaving substantial gap to human performance. The current formulation also focuses primarily on adapting locomotion to the follower. more natural robot leader could additionally communicate during interaction, for example by turning toward waiting follower, using gestures, or providing verbal prompts before resuming the task. Future work can therefore extend follower-aware route execution toward richer, more proactive and communicative leading while improving spatial robustness, referent grounding, and interaction modeling. We will release LeadVLA checkpoints, LeadInfra, LeadBench, and evaluation tools as an open research stack for continued exploration of richer robot-leading behaviors.

LeadVLA uses synchronized frontand rear-view RGB observations to capture both local route-execution context and the evolving state of the follower. For each view, we use the current frame together with five historical frames approximately uniformly sampled from the preceding 31 simulation frames, covering about 3.1 of temporal context at 10 Hz. This results in 12 RGB images per policy query. At the beginning of an episode, unavailable history is filled by repeating the earliest available frame. All images are resized to 384 384 before being processed by the multimodal backbone. The two views share the same multimodal backbone rather than using camera-specific visual encoders. We use fixed input order and explicitly identify the view roles in the instruction: the first six images correspond to the front-view history and current observation, and the following six correspond to the rear view. Language-conditioned referent, interaction intent, and route. The language instruction specifies both who to lead and how to lead. In multi-person settings, the designated follower is specified through naturallanguage appearance description, while the requested distance and relative formation are expressed in the same instruction. Referent grounding is learned jointly from appearance-conditioned LeadInfra instructions, target-related semantic supervision, and the controlled referent interventions described in Sec. 3.4; no external person-recognition or ReID supervision is used. compact local route hint is serialized directly as robot-local coordinates and inserted into the language prompt, with denoting the forward direction and the leftward direction. The predicted semantics are not assembled into an explicit follower-state vector that is subsequently passed to separate controller. Instead, their supervision directly shapes the shared action representation from which Pace and Residual are decoded. Target localization encourages grounding of the language-designated follower; lateral and distance encode relative geometry; observation captures target presence, loss, and reacquisition; motion describes the followers movement state; and formation indicates whether the requested spatial relation is being acquired, maintained, or corrected. The representation therefore retains rich visual and temporal information while being explicitly supervised for follower-relevant structure. Configurable interaction semantics. The supervised spatial relations are defined by the interaction contract used to generate the data, rather than as universal social conventions. The metric ranges associated with near/far distance and the angular ranges associated with left/center/right formation are configurable in LeadInfra. LeadVLA therefore learns the interaction relations instantiated by the training contract rather than assuming that fixed metric distance or bearing is universally near, far, left, or right. For the experiments in this paper, we use one fixed configuration for training and evaluation; its numerical definition is provided in Sec. B.3. Selective semantic coupling. All six objectives shape the shared control representation during training, but only the soft lateral and formation predictions are given an additional direct pathway to Residual. Their predicted distributions are mapped by the semantic fusion module into sample-level modulation, which is broadcast to the horizon-wise Residual queries before trajectory decoding. Using soft distributions preserves prediction uncertainty and keeps the coupling differentiable. Target localization, distance, observation, and motion have no direct action-fusion pathway and affect action only through the shared representation. Pace is likewise decoded from the original action queries without explicit semantic fusion. The output layer of the semantic fusion module is initialized to zero, so the fusion initially contributes no modulation and training begins from the unfused Residual pathway. The major asset groups are summarized in Table 10 and visualized in Fig. 7. Environments and maps. LeadInfra covers approximately 65,198 m2 of navigable indoor and outdoor space, including parks, playgrounds, residential areas, offices, exhibition spaces, restaurants, and parking areas. Each environment is accompanied by metric GridMap at 0.5 m/cell resolution, providing common spatial representation for route generation and scene construction. Embodied and human assets. The infrastructure supports three representative robot embodiments: Unitree G1 humanoid, Scout Mini wheeled robot, and quadruped robot-dog platform. For followers and distractors, LeadInfra provides 756 compatibility-validated human appearance configurations composed from variations in body, clothing, accessories, and body scale. This appearance diversity supports languageconditioned target designation in multi-person interactions. Sensing and physical scene assets. LeadInfra provides 25 sensor blueprints spanning camera, LiDAR, and state-sensing modalities, together with 142 reusable static objects for constructing scene interference, occlusion, and local route variation. These numbers describe the capability of the infrastructure rather than the observation space of LeadVLA: the policy studied in this work uses only the front/rear RGB observations and task inputs described in Sec. A.1, while additional sensing modalities are used only for data construction, supervision, or evaluation where required. B.2 Route Generation and Scene Variation Route generation. LeadInfra generates nominal routes from the metric navigability representation of each environment. Starting from the 0.5 m/cell GridMap introduced in Sec. B.1, the route generator samples feasible anchors in navigable space, connects them through collision-free paths, and smooths the resulting trajectories into arc-length-parameterized routes (s). Routes are filtered for traversability, clearance, continuity, and curvature, while geometrically redundant routes are removed to reduce repeated sampling of the same spatial corridor. The resulting collection contains approximately 1K nominal routes spanning six representative geometry families: straight, single-turn, S-shaped, multi-turn, U-turn, and loop trajectories. Route geometry is varied independently from follower interaction programs, allowing similar events such as lagging, stopping, or reacquisition to occur across different route structures. This discourages the policy from associating particular follower response with fixed trajectory pattern and instead exposes follower-aware adaptation across diverse route executions. Nominal route and local scene variation. Each episode is anchored by nominal route that remains fixed throughout execution. LeadInfra then varies the local physical conditions under which this route must In selected episodes, static objects or pedestrians create local route interference, requiring be executed. temporary deviation from the nominal route followed by recovery toward it. These cases couple local route adaptation with follower-aware interaction. For example, temporary deviation may alter robotfollower distance and bearing, change the rear-view observation, or briefly occlude the designated follower. The policy must therefore adapt locally while preserving both the nominal route reference and appropriate follower-aware behavior. These variations are intended to study route recovery under interaction rather than to define general-purpose obstacle-avoidance task. Route information boundary. The learned policy always receives the original nominal route as its route input. For data generation, LeadInfra may internally construct episode-specific collision-free execution references for the causal expert and the physical motion of human actors. These privileged execution references are never exposed to the learned policy. The policy therefore receives neither an expert detour nor an obstacleconditioned replacement route or local-planning output. Any local deviation must consequently be inferred from policy-visible observations while the nominal route remains the persistent task-level spatial reference. This information boundary directly matches the structured formulation of LeadVLA: Path preserves the nominal route, while learned Pace and Residual determine how that route is executed under follower and local scene variation. B.3 Follower Interaction Programs LeadInfra structures follower interaction along three complementary dimensions: motion, presence, and requested formation. These factors are configurable and can be composed with different routes and scenes, subject to physical and semantic compatibility. This allows similar follower events to occur under diverse execution conditions rather than being tied to particular route or scene. Follower motion programs. We define eight representative temporal motion programs covering stable tracking, different degrees of lagging and slowdown, hesitation, stopping, recovery, and failure to initiate. Each program specifies behavior pattern with randomized timing and motion parameters rather than fixed follower trajectory. The programs are summarized in Table 11. The program labels control only the simulated follower behavior and are not directly mapped to robot actions. Robot supervision is generated from the realized physical consequences of these programs, such as sustained separation or loss of target observability, as detailed in Sec. B.5. Presence and reacquisition. Motion variation is complemented by explicit target-presence conditions. LeadInfra distinguishes follower that slows or falls behind while remaining observable from one that becomes temporarily or persistently unobservable. We use five representative conditions, summarized in Table 12. These conditions introduce temporal ambiguity that cannot be resolved from single observation. For example, temporary occlusion during local route adaptation should not necessarily trigger immediate waiting, Table 11 Follower-motion programs in LeadInfra. Likewise, continued visibility of distractor must not substitute for the missing target. Configurable interaction contract. LeadInfra also varies the requested robotfollower relation through language-conditioned distance and formation specifications. These relations are configurable interaction requirements rather than universal social-distance conventions. For the experiments in this paper, we use the fixed configuration in Table 13. Combining two distance relations with three relative formations yields six language-conditioned formation settings. These interaction-contract definitions are used to construct follower-related semantic supervision and the corresponding benchmark conditions. Thus, LeadVLA learns the interaction contract instantiated by the data rather than assuming universally correct metric distance or bearing. B.4 Referent-Aware Interaction LeadInfra constructs multi-person interactions in which one person is designated as the follower through language while other nearby people act as distractors. This allows follower-conditioned control to be supervised with respect to the current language referent rather than unrelated distractor behavior in the scene. In multi-person episodes, the policy-visible target designation Appearance-conditioned target designation. is provided through natural-language appearance description together with the requested distance and formation. No target ID, ground-truth bounding box, person trajectory, or simulator identity is exposed to the policy. Target and distractor appearances are selected to remain distinguishable under their corresponding language descriptions, using the human appearance assets introduced in Sec. B.1. Counterfactual referent pairs. We construct matched episode pairs that preserve the environment, nominal route, human actors, initial configuration, sensing conditions, and human behavior, while changing which person is designated by the language instruction. For example, one person may execute stoprecover behavior while another continues steady tracking. If the stopping person is the target, the resulting interaction should induce slowing or waiting; if the other person is designated instead, the same stop becomes distractor event and should not modulate the robot response. Dynamic target reassignment. Selected episodes additionally change the designated follower once during execution. When the new target satisfies predefined visibility and formation-compatibility conditions, the target and distractor roles are atomically reassigned and the language instruction is updated to describe the new follower. No explicit switch state or target identifier is provided to the policy; it simply receives the updated ordinary leading instruction. The previously designated follower remains in the scene after reassignment and continues moving, but should no longer determine the robot response. Conversely, subsequent behavior of the newly designated follower should now influence execution. This complements the counterfactual pairs by requiring referent-conditioned control to update online rather than remain attached to persistent person identity. Together, counterfactual referent pairs and dynamic reassignment provide the referent-aware co-training supervision described in Sec. 3.4. B.5 Causal Expert Supervision LeadInfra uses scripted follower programs to generate controlled interaction events, but these hidden programs are never mapped directly to robot actions. Instead, the programs first produce physical follower behavior in simulation, and the expert reacts only to interaction evidence that has already been realized: hidden follower program realized physical interaction expert robot action. The expert may use simulator-derived information describing the current realized interaction, including robot follower geometry, target observability, robot state, and local scene feasibility. Latent behavior labels, future schedules, and upcoming interaction transitions are excluded from the reaction logic. Robot trajectories are generated online in closed loop from the current realized state rather than replayed from precomputed action scripts. Distance-driven Pace supervision. Follower separation is measured along the current execution route rather than by Euclidean distance. Let gt = srobot starget denote the robottarget arc-length separation. At the transition from setup to leading, the realized separation is recorded as baseline g0. After dynamic target reassignment, the baseline is reset according to the newly requested formation. To suppress short-term motion noise, the expert maintains an exponentially smoothed separation, gt = gt1 + α (gt gt1) , α = 1 exp(t/0.5), corresponding to 0.5 time constant. We define the realized separation drift as dt = gt g0. The expert begins reducing Pace only when dt > 0.25 persists for at least 0.5 s. For sustained drift, the target Pace scale is zt = clip (cid:18) dt 0.25 1.25 0.25 (cid:19) , 0, 1 , agt = 1 z2 (3 2zt). Thus, the target remains at full Pace for small separation changes, decreases smoothly as the follower falls behind, and reaches zero when the drift reaches 1.25 m. The resulting expert motion is rate-limited with acceleration and deceleration bounds of 0.5 and 0.6 m/s2, respectively, at the nominal leading speed of 0.75 m/s. Target loss and reacquisition. Target observability provides second source of causal interaction evidence. When the designated follower first becomes unobservable, the expert enters conservative temporary-missing regime rather than stopping immediately. During this period, the Pace target is capped at 0.65. If the target remains continuously missing for 0.8 or the robot travels 0.6 without observing the target, whichever occurs first, the expert transitions to waiting and reduces the target Pace to zero through smooth braking transition. When the same target reappears, it must remain continuously observable for 0.5 before normal leading resumes. new disappearance during this confirmation period returns the expert to waiting. Resumption is likewise rate-limited rather than applied as an instantaneous speed change. Temporary occlusion caused by static scene geometry is treated separately from persistent target loss. Such occlusions retain their visibility and occlusion supervision, but short static occlusions do not directly trigger the persistent-loss stopping logic in the final data collection. This distinction exposes the policy to cases in which the follower is briefly unobservable during local route adaptation without teaching it to stop at every transient occlusion. Causal supervision boundary. These rules depend only on interaction evidence available after it has physically occurred. For example, scripted stop does not immediately reduce the expert Pace; the response emerges only after the realized robotfollower separation exceeds the reaction threshold. Similarly, target loss affects the expert only after sustained absence or blind travel is observed. The resulting supervision therefore preserves precise simulator-based control while avoiding shortcut mappings from hidden follower programs or future interaction schedules to robot actions. B.6 Data Scale and Composition The current LeadInfra corpus contains approximately 4M training samples collected over roughly 1K nominal routes. Unlike short isolated clips, episodes are temporally extended closed-loop interactions that may contain multiple follower events and repeated transitions among leading, slowing, waiting, and recovery. Table 14 summarizes the scale and major variation dimensions of the current training corpus. Route length refers to the nominal-route arc length and excludes additional travel caused by local scenedependent deviations. Long episodes allow multiple interaction events to occur within single rollout, exposing the policy to repeated adaptation and recovery while route execution continues. The motion, presence, and formation dimensions define 8 5 6 = 240 nominal interaction combinations before route geometry, human appearance, referent configuration, and scene variation are considered. These factors are composed subject to physical and semantic compatibility rather than exhaustively enumerated as Cartesian product. The reported statistics describe the current training instantiation rather than the capacity of LeadInfra. Its route generator, interaction programs, formation specifications, actor assets, and scene recipes remain configurable, allowing additional training conditions to be generated without changing the infrastructure.

Each episode is specified before policy execution so that different methods face the same task condition rather than policy-dependent environment variation. The benchmark uses held-out environments, routes, human actors, and scene instantiations that are disjoint from LeadInfra training, while preserving the same task definition and interaction contract. It also fixes the runtime configuration and terminal conditions required for reproducible closed-loop evaluation. The manifest defines the evaluation condition but does not expose privileged supervision to the policy. Hidden follower behavior states, ground-truth target annotations, privileged detour paths, future interaction schedules, and expert actions are excluded from policy-visible inputs. In multi-person evaluation, matched counterfactual rollouts preserve the underlying route, actors, interaction program, and scene configuration while changing the language-designated target, as detailed in Sec. C.2. C.2 Counterfactual Multi-Person Evaluation Multi-person cases use matched target-A/target-B counterfactual rollouts to evaluate whether the robot responds to the language-designated follower rather than to unrelated nearby people. Within each matched pair, the nominal route, human appearances, initial layout, requested formation, behavior program, and scene configuration are kept fixed. Only the language-designated target and the corresponding target/distractor roles used for evaluation are exchanged. Thus, the same physical behavior should influence the robot when produced by the designated follower, but should be ignored when produced by distractor. Each matched target-A/target-B pair is first aggregated into single logical multi-person case before benchmark-level statistics are computed. Single-person rollouts directly form individual logical cases. This prevents multi-person conditions from receiving additional weight simply because referent attribution requires two matched physical rollouts. C.3 Common Runtime and Fairness LeadBench evaluates all methods under the same frozen episode conditions and shared execution environment. For each episode, the environment initialization, robot embodiment, sensing setup, nominal robot route, follower reference route, follower appearance and behavior, scene configuration, and environment-side execution conditions are kept fixed across policies. Methods may retain their native action representations, inference frequencies, and model-specific preprocessing. Evaluation is fully closed loop: each policy output changes the subsequent robot state and therefore the observations available at the next decision step. Fairness is enforced through matched task conditions, common policy-visible information boundary, and the same execution environment, rather than by forcing identical internal model interfaces. No evaluated method receives privileged simulator information such as ground-truth target state, hidden behavior labels, future interaction schedules, expert actions, or privileged detour paths. sections.content: D.1 Baseline Adaptation and Fairness We adapt representative baselines to LeadBench while preserving the core modeling paradigm of each reference method. When official implementations or checkpoints are available, we build on them directly; otherwise, we implement task-adapted versions that retain the corresponding perception, interaction, and control structure while modifying only the interfaces required for robot-leading evaluation. These baselines are intended to represent their respective modeling paradigms under common robot-leading setting rather than to reproduce the original evaluation environments of the reference methods. All trainable baselines use LeadInfra for task-specific training or fine-tuning when applicable, whereas the classical Fiore-style controller requires no learned leading policy. For modular baselines, we use Grounding DINO Tiny [34] for language-conditioned person grounding and Depth Anything V2 Small [35] where monocular depth cues are required. Uni-NaVid [27] is initialized from its released checkpoint and fine-tuned on LeadInfra. Table 17 summarizes the resulting implementations. All methods are evaluated under the same frozen LeadBench conditions and policy-visible information boundary described in Appendix C.3. The reported Human Expert results are obtained by averaging each LeadBench metric across the three operators. Human Expert is reported as reference rather than included in the robot-policy ranking. Across the evaluated conditions, human performance remains substantially stronger on joint task completion and interactionoriented metrics, while still falling below perfect TRS and SCS. Human RF can also be slightly lower than that of strong route-following controllers because teleoperation introduces small deviations from the nominal route. The human reference therefore provides practical reference point under the same observation setting rather than metric-perfect upper bound. D.3 Additional Ablation Analysis Structured route execution across difficulty. The aggregate results in the main paper establish the overall benefit of structured route execution. Table 18 further reports LSR across LeadBench difficulty levels, averaging the singleand multi-person conditions within each level. Replacing direct trajectory prediction with Path + Pace produces the largest gain under Core conditions, increasing LSR from 0.292 to 0.646. This indicates that explicitly retaining the nominal route provides strong execution prior when little local route recovery is required. The role of Residual becomes more evident as route interference increases: adding Residual changes Core LSR from 0.646 to 0.604, but improves Easy from 0.229 to 0.312 and Constrained from 0.188 to 0.271. Together with the aggregate RF results in the main paper, this reveals the intended trade-off. Path + Pace most strongly preserves nominal route execution, whereas Residual sacrifices some strict route fidelity in exchange for stronger task completion when local deviation and recovery become necessary. The benefit of the full formulation therefore becomes more apparent under harder route-interference conditions rather than simply reflecting uniformly more flexible trajectory decoder. Real-World Evaluation and Qualitative Analysis E.1 Real-Robot Setup and Evaluation Protocol Robot and sensing. We deploy LeadVLA on Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with frontand rear-facing Intel RealSense D455 cameras, as shown in Fig. 11. The policy interface is kept consistent with simulation: LeadVLA receives front/rear RGB observations, the language instruction, and the frozen nominal route. Depth observations are not provided to the policy and are retained only for offline evaluation of the Social Contract Score (SCS). Physical locomotion is executed through the native Unitree G1 controller. Global-route construction. For each environment, we first construct map using SLAM. destination is then selected and nominal global route is planned with ROS move_base. Once generated, this route is frozen for the full episode and transformed into the robot-local route representation required by LeadVLA at each policy query. The nominal route is not replanned during policy execution. Closed-loop deployment. Robot sensing and policy inference are connected through WebSocket communication. At each policy query, the robot sends its current front/rear RGB observations and route context to the inference server. LeadVLA returns 24-step robot-local waypoint trajectory, which is passed to the robot-side trajectory-tracking interface and executed through the G1 locomotion controller. The downstream controller tracks the trajectory predicted by LeadVLA but does not generate an obstacle-conditioned replacement route or modify the frozen nominal route. In particular, no obstacle replanning is performed during policy execution. Local deviations around route interference must therefore originate from the trajectory predicted by LeadVLA rather than from downstream navigation planner. These failures therefore expose remaining limitation in visually grounded local trajectory adaptation under physical route interference. Improving this capability while preserving follower-aware execution is an important direction for future work. Formation transfer is uneven. LeadVLA retains visible notion of the requested interaction geometry after sim-to-real transfer. Changing near/far instructions produces observable changes in robotfollower distance, which are also reflected in the depth-based SCS evaluation. Lateral formation transfer is weaker: when instructed to lead with the follower on the left or right, the physical robot often keeps the follower closer to the center of the rear-view image rather than maintaining pronounced lateral offset. This observation suggests that fine-grained lateral formation may require more precise visual spatial reasoning than longitudinal distance regulation. Because LeadVLA learns these relations directly from RGB observations without real-world policy fine-tuning or additional geometric supervision, lateral formation remains challenging component of sim-to-real transfer. We treat this as qualitative observation rather than separate quantitative claim, as we do not perform dedicated real-world lateral-formation study. Physical deployment introduces additional domain gaps. Humanoid locomotion introduces camera vibration that is largely absent from the simulation observations, adding temporal visual noise to both front and rear streams. Communication and inference latency can also delay the robots response to rapid changes in follower behavior. Across the evaluated settings, route fidelity remains comparatively strong, while finer-grained local adaptation, referent grounding, and lateral formation become more challenging under physical deployment. These observations suggest that future improvements should focus less on recovering the nominal route itself and more on robustly adapting its execution under real-world visual, interaction, and control uncertainty. The distractor begins to lag, stops, and eventually falls substantially behind in the later frames, while LeadVLA continues leading Target without slowing or waiting for the distractor. sections.title: F Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Despite relatively strong route fidelity, several aspects of follower-aware adaptation remain challenging. First, local spatial adaptation is still limited when route interference must be handled jointly with follower response. Our real-world experiments show that failures in the Easy settings are frequently associated with insufficient deviation and recovery around local interference, indicating that stronger visual spatial reasoning is needed to better coordinate route recovery with human-aware execution. The current evaluation also focuses primarily on static or structured local interference; more general interaction with dynamic obstacles remains an important extension. Second, fine-grained formation control transfers less reliably than route-level execution. Distance-conditioned behavior remains observable in physical deployment, whereas left/right formation is more difficult to maintain. This suggests that lateral formation places greater demands on precise visual spatial reasoning and geometryaware control than coarse longitudinal distance regulation. Third, referent-aware control remains sensitive to visual ambiguity. The policy can condition its behavior on the designated follower when appearance cues are sufficiently distinguishable, but visually similar target and distractor appearances can still lead to ambiguous target binding and occasional distractor interference. Harder appearance-matched counterfactuals, stronger temporal identity consistency, and richer multi-person interaction patterns may further improve referent attribution. The current formulation also adapts primarily through locomotion. more capable robot leader could communicate proactively through viewpoint changes, body orientation, gestures, or verbal prompts, rather than relying only on slowing, waiting, and trajectory adjustment. Extending the action space toward such communicative behaviors would allow future systems to study not only how the robot reacts to follower state, but also how it can actively shape the interaction. More broadly, the remaining gap on LeadBench suggests that future robot-leading policies should move beyond purely reactive adaptation. Predictive modeling of follower motion could allow the robot to anticipate lagging, formation drift, or temporary disengagement, and adjust its pace and local motion before the interaction becomes difficult to recover. We therefore view stronger spatial reasoning, referent grounding, predictive human-motion modeling, and proactive communication as complementary extensions to the current structured formulation. The central hypothesis remains that route-level task intent can be kept explicit and stable while learning progressively richer ways of adapting its execution to evolving human and scene conditions.
